--- title: "Prediction versus explanation" description: "Two different scientific goals that pull models in different directions, and why the best predictor is rarely the best explanation." order: 4 categories: [foundations, interpretation] --- ## The cost of an unstated goal Almost every disappointing machine-learning project in marine science begins with a goal that was never stated. Someone wants to know *why* a species is declining, builds a model that predicts well, and then discovers that it will not answer the question. The two goals are genuinely different: - **Prediction**: given conditions I have not observed, what will the value be? - **Explanation**: how does this driver affect the outcome, and by how much? A model can be superb at one and useless at the other. Worse, nothing in the output warns you: a model with an excellent test score looks equally impressive whichever question you brought. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## The idea Think about what each goal permits. For **prediction**, any variable that carries information is fair game. Whether it causes the outcome is irrelevant. If bird sightings predict fish abundance, use bird sightings. Distance from port, survey vessel, day of year are all legitimate, provided they will be available when you deploy the model and mean the same thing then. For **explanation**, the variable must play the right causal role, and which *other* variables you include changes the answer. Add the wrong covariate and the effect you care about shifts, vanishes, or reverses. Explanation requires you to think about the system; prediction lets you avoid thinking about it. There is a second asymmetry, which is less often said out loud: ::: {.callout-note} For prediction, you can check whether you succeeded: hold data back and measure. For explanation, you usually cannot. There is no held-out dataset that tells you whether your estimate of the temperature effect is the true one. You have arguments, assumptions and design, and that is all. ::: This is why "the model predicts well, so the effects must be right" is not a valid inference. It is also why a model built for explanation should be judged on whether its structure matches the science, not on its test score. ## Worked example Four models on the same data. Two are shaped by thinking about the species; two are shaped by letting the algorithm work. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey() split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) plain <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate # An ecologist's model: species have thermal and depth optima, so allow curves. curved <- abundance ~ poly(depth_m, 2) + poly(temperature_c, 2) + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate # A predictor's model: throw in position, which is not a cause of anything. located <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + longitude + latitude forest <- function(formula) { rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |> set_mode("regression") |> fit(formula, data = train) } fits <- list( "Linear model" = linear_reg() |> fit(plain, data = train), "Linear model, with curves" = linear_reg() |> fit(curved, data = train), "Random forest" = forest(plain), "Random forest + coordinates" = forest(located) ) imap(fits, \(fit, name) { augment(fit, test) |> rmse(truth = abundance, estimate = .pred) |> transmute(model = name, test_rmse = round(.estimate, 2)) }) |> list_rbind() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | test_rmse| |:---------------------------|---------:| |Linear model | 4.22| |Linear model, with curves | 4.01| |Random forest | 4.13| |Random forest + coordinates | 3.98|
::: ::: Read that ranking carefully, because it is not the one people expect. The **linear model with curved terms predicts better than the random forest**, and almost as well as the forest with coordinates added. The best-performing interpretable model here came not from a more powerful algorithm but from one piece of ecology: species have optima, so let the relationship bend. And what does that model say about temperature, the variable the plain linear model dismissed? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tidy(fits[["Linear model, with curves"]]) |> filter(grepl("temperature", term)) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |poly(temperature_c, 2)1 | -4.368| 4.780| -0.914| 0.361| |poly(temperature_c, 2)2 | -30.251| 4.502| -6.720| 0.000|
::: ::: The linear term is still not significant. The quadratic term is overwhelmingly so. The "no temperature effect" from [the second page](what-is-machine-learning.qmd) was never a fact about the species. It was a fact about a model that could only draw straight lines. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grid <- tibble( temperature_c = seq(3, 16, by = 0.05), depth_m = median(train$depth_m), chlorophyll_mg_m3 = median(train$chlorophyll_mg_m3), salinity_psu = median(train$salinity_psu), substrate = factor("sand", levels = levels(train$substrate)) ) grid$predicted <- predict(fits[["Linear model, with curves"]], new_data = grid)$.pred fitted_optimum <- grid$temperature_c[which.max(grid$predicted)] ggplot(grid, aes(temperature_c, predicted)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 9, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.8) + geom_vline(xintercept = fitted_optimum, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) + geom_line(colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], linewidth = 1.2) + annotate("text", x = 9.25, y = min(grid$predicted), hjust = 0, label = "true optimum, 9 °C", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], size = 3.6) + annotate("text", x = 8.35, y = max(grid$predicted), hjust = 1, label = paste0("fitted, ", round(fitted_optimum, 1), " °C"), colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.6) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Predicted abundance", title = "An interpretable model, recovering something true") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The temperature response recovered by the curved model, with other variables held at their median. The fitted optimum (dashed) sits at 8.6 °C; the value built into the simulation (solid) is 9 °C.](prediction-and-explanation_files/figure-html/fig-optimum-1.png){#fig-optimum fig-alt='A curve of predicted abundance against temperature rising from about 3 degrees to a peak just below 9 degrees and falling away to 16 degrees. A dashed vertical line marks the fitted optimum at 8.6 degrees and a solid vertical line marks the true optimum at 9 degrees; the two nearly coincide.' width=1400} ::: ::: Because this dataset is simulated, we can do what real data never allows: check the answer. The species really does peak at 9 °C, and the model says 8.6 °C. It recovered the ecology. Notice also what the curve does at its ends: it predicts *negative* abundance below about 3 °C and above about 15 °C. Counts cannot be negative. We fitted a linear model to count data, and this is the price: the interpretation is sound near the centre of the data and nonsense at the edges. [Section 3](../03-supervised-learning/index.qmd) fixes this properly with a model built for counts. It is worth seeing the flaw first: a model can recover a real biological optimum and still make impossible predictions, and a plot of only the central range would have hidden it. ## Reading the four models Now look at the model that predicted best: the forest with longitude and latitude added. Those two coordinates improved prediction. They are also, ecologically, nothing. No fish responds to longitude. What they do is act as a **proxy**: they let the model absorb spatial structure that the environmental variables fail to capture. The model has effectively learned *where the good patches were during this survey*. For prediction inside the surveyed area, in the surveyed period, that is legitimate and useful. As explanation it is empty, and if anyone extracts a variable-importance plot from it and reports that "position is the strongest driver of abundance", they have said nothing about the species at all. So we have three models and three different kinds of answer: | Model | Predicts | Explains | Honest use | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Plain linear model | Worst | Misleadingly: reports no temperature effect | None here; the form is wrong | | Linear model with curves | Nearly best | Yes, recovers the 9 °C optimum | Either goal | | Random forest | Middling | No coefficients to read | Prediction, with care | | Forest + coordinates | Best | No, position is a proxy, not a cause | Prediction inside the surveyed area only | The best predictor is the worst explanation. The best explanation is nearly the best predictor. Neither of those is a general law, but both are common enough that assuming the opposite is a real risk. ## Limits of this separation **"Interpretable" is not the same as "correct".** The curved model gave a clean temperature optimum, and we verified it only because we wrote the simulation. With real data, an interpretable model can be confidently, legibly wrong, and its legibility makes it more persuasive, not less. **Proxies are not always obvious.** Longitude is easy to spot. Sampling date standing in for a survey-design change, or a sensor serial number standing in for calibration drift, is not, and both will improve your test score. **Explanation has prerequisites that no algorithm supplies.** Which covariates to include is a causal question, answered with subject knowledge, not by trying combinations and keeping the best score. [Section 10](../10-interpretation/index.qmd) returns to this with the tools for it. **A recovered effect can sit inside an impossible model.** The curved model found the thermal optimum and predicts negative abundance at both extremes. Getting one thing right is not a certificate for the rest, and the parts of a model you do not plot are the parts that embarrass you later. **Prediction has an expiry date.** A model that learned where the good patches were is valid while the patches stay put. Under a shifting climate, the proxy silently stops being a proxy, and the model gives no signal that anything has changed. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Decide which question you are asking *before* choosing a method. Prediction and explanation pull in different directions. - For prediction, any informative variable is fair. For explanation, the variable has to play the right causal role, and the other covariates change the answer. - You can verify prediction by holding data back. You cannot verify explanation the same way, which is why a good test score is not evidence that your effects are real. - Subject knowledge often beats algorithmic flexibility: knowing that species have thermal optima was worth more here than 500 trees. - A variable that improves prediction can be ecologically meaningless. Position is the clearest case, and variable-importance plots will still rank it at the top. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Fit the forest with coordinates but *without* depth and temperature. How much does prediction suffer? What does that tell you about how much the coordinates were standing in for? 2. Take the curved model and drop `salinity_psu`. Do the other coefficients move? Now imagine you had no way to know salinity was irrelevant, which is the normal situation, and consider what that implies for reporting effect sizes.
